newsitem.title: UK: Britain's FTSE leaps to new record as rates worries recede.
newsitem.headline: Britain's FTSE leaps to new record as rates worries recede.

text.p: The British stock market took its cue from an ever buoyant Wall Street and leapt into uncharted territory on Tuesday, casting aside political and interest rate concerns.
The benchmark FT-SE 100 index of blue-chip shares jumped by 60.9 points, or 1.5 percent, to an all-time closing high of 4,168.2, building on Monday's 50.7 point advance.
In the past two days the gains in the FT-SE 100 have added some 18 billion pounds ($30.11 billion) to its value.
The advance came as the Dow raced to a record peak for the fourth consecutive session in early U.S. trading, propelled by a lower-than-expected increase in December U.S. consumer prices.
The figures boosted hopes for steady non-inflationary growth through 1997 on both sides of the Atlantic.

"The golden scenario is here. We have had a big run though into new high ground. Th US figures have confirmed the picture of solid growth with low inflation and it looks as if we will get away without a rate rise in the UK tomorrow," said one trader. "It is all looking rather good."

British monetary authorities meet on Wednesday amid growing expectations that a rate rise may be avoided, a view bolstered by the release of tame UK inflation figures on Monday and as Christmas sales data showed no sign of a runaway consumer spree.

"All of the data and all of the anecdotal evidence I hear suggests there are no price pressures and no pressures in the pipeline," said David Bruce, managing director at Abbey life Investment Services.
The appreciation of sterling has kept a lid on import prices and Christmas sales were not quite as strong as many had expected, he noted.
Recent gains have come as a surprise to many who believed the market would struggle to make ground early this year as British interest rates looked poised to rise.

Yet big investment funds, flush with cash, have snapped up shares this week in British banks, insurers, food retailers and other domestic-related issues, bolstering trading volumes. By 1640 GMT, almost 888 million shares were registered.

"The market has been good following Wall Street," said the head of equity trading at one brokerage, "people want to buy and there is a shortage of stock in the market. It is just weight of money, pure and simple."
Risks however remain.
"The biggest risk to the rally in the UK is either a signficant political storm here or a correction in the U.S.," said David Aserkoff, a strategist with Credit Suisse First Boston.
"The latter is probably more likely, but the question is how likely are either of those things? It's a benign environment for stocks," he said.
Uncertainty surrounding the policies of the Labour Party, well placed to win the next election, is also expected to cast a shadow over the market in the medium term, strategists said.
On Tuesday interest-rate sensitive issues fared best, but gains were broad based, with FTSE 100 advancers outpacing decliners by a margin of seven to three.
Bank shares continued to forge ahead after outperforming the market in 1996, with investors still lured by the promise of steady growth and low inflation. Many in the sector ended at new highs.

Abbey National shares surged 27p to 800-1/2p, having reached a new peak at 802. Shares in Lloyds climbed 21-1/2p to 479-1/2, 1-1/2p off the record high set earlier. Shares in Standard Chartered Bank added 20p to 713-1/2p, while shares in Barclays soared 28-1/2p to 1110-1/2, having reached a record peak at 1112. Natwest shares jumped 24p to 782-1/2.

The insurance sector also advance. Shares in Prudential Corp jumped 23p to 537, while Britaannic shares rose 15p to 780. United Assurance gained 11-1/2p to 515. Legal and General was flat at 393-1/2p, having risen earlier.

The insurance sector been bolstered in recent months by expections of further consolidation, said Richard Jeffrey, head of research at Charterhouse Tilney. "But people are also positive about business margins and volumes," he added.
Elsewhere, investors shifted into safer supermarket shares from the store sector after Christmas retail sales fell short of expectations, analysts said. ($1=.5979 Pound)
